\begin{frame}{Today's question and route}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: two prices both wander like random walks; can a combination of them be stable, and how do we model it?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if yes, the series share a common stochastic trend and a long-run equilibrium: regressions in levels are meaningful, not spurious
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Route} of the chapter
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the idea of cointegration; the Engle--Granger two-step method with the right critical values; error correction models
        \item the VECM and the Granger representation theorem; the Johansen tests; estimating and reading $\beta$ and $\alpha$; forecasting
        \item applications: purchasing power parity, interest rates, three Central European currencies, pairs trading on the Bucharest Stock Exchange
    \end{itemize}
    \item We build on \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3} (unit roots, spurious regression) and \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6} (VAR models); Seminar 7 comes before this lecture
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

%=============================================================================
\section{The idea of cointegration}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{From spurious regression to cointegration}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}: regressing one $I(1)$ series on another, \textbf{unrelated} $I(1)$ series gives large $t$, high $R^2$ and a Durbin--Watson statistic near 0 \refGN
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the error $y_t - a - b x_t$ is itself $I(1)$ for every $b$: nothing ties the two series together
    \end{itemize}
    \item The exception: for one value of $b$, the combination $u_t = y_t - a - b x_t$ is \textbf{stationary}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item then $y_t$ and $x_t$ are \textbf{cointegrated} \refGranger, \refEG: the regression in levels estimates a real long-run relation
        \item the two series may drift apart for a while, but $u_t$ always pulls them back: an \textbf{equilibrium}
    \end{itemize}
    \item Today: how to recognise this case, how to test it, and how to model it
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A drunk and her dog}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.38\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.40\textheight]{ch7_dog_walking_2018.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{A walk with a dog: two paths that never drift far apart}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dog_walking_woman.jpg}{Photo: Amin (2018); CC BY-SA 4.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \refMurray: a drunk leaves the pub and wanders: her path $x_t$ is a random walk
    \begin{itemize}
        \item her dog also wanders: $y_t$ is a random walk too
        \item the distance between two \textbf{independent} walkers grows without limit, like $\sqrt{t}$
    \end{itemize}
    \item But the dog hears her call and runs back; she hears the dog and turns towards it
    \begin{itemize}
        \item each corrects part of the gap: $\Delta x_t = c\,(y_{t-1} - x_{t-1}) + u_t$, $\Delta y_t = d\,(x_{t-1} - y_{t-1}) + w_t$; $c, d > 0$: the shares of the gap closed per step; $u_t$, $w_t$: independent shocks
        \item both paths remain unpredictable, but the distance $y_t - x_t$ stays bounded: \textbf{cointegration} with \textbf{error correction}
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The drunk and her dog by simulation}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.56\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_drunk_dog.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the simulation: the distances}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Each path is $I(1)$: ADF on $x_t$ gives p = 0.21
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the distance $y_t - x_t$ is an AR(1) with $\rho = 1 - c - d = 0.6$: ADF p $<$\,0.001, standard deviation 1.9
        \item the distance to the stray dog wanders: ADF p = 0.81, standard deviation 14.1
    \end{itemize}
    \item Half of a gap disappears in $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.6 = 1.4$ steps: the \textbf{half-life} (Section 3)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item knowing where the drunk is tells us where to look for the dog, even though neither path can be forecast
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Definition of cointegration}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Definition} \refEG: the components of $\mathbf y_t = (y_{1t}, \dots, y_{nt})^\top$ are \textbf{cointegrated of order (1,1)}, $\mathbf y_t \sim CI(1,1)$, if
    \begin{itemize}
        \item every component is $I(1)$ (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}: stationary after one difference), and
        \item some linear combination $\beta^\top \mathbf y_t$, with $\beta \neq 0$, is $I(0)$: stationary
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\beta$ is the \textbf{cointegrating vector}; $u_t = \beta^\top \mathbf y_t - \mu$ is the \textbf{equilibrium error} ($\mu$: its mean; $\top$: transpose)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\beta$ is unique only up to scale: $2\beta$ works as well; we \textbf{normalise} one coefficient to 1, e.g.\ $\beta = (1, -b)^\top$
        \item with $n$ variables there can be up to $r = n - 1$ independent cointegrating vectors; $r$ is the \textbf{cointegration rank}
    \end{itemize}
    \item Cointegration is a property of the \textbf{levels}: differencing the data destroys the information in $\beta^\top \mathbf y_t$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Common stochastic trends}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Write $x_t = x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ (a random walk) and $y_t = b\,x_t + u_t$, with $u_t$ stationary
    \begin{itemize}
        \item both series contain the same stochastic trend $\sum_{s \le t} \varepsilon_s$; $y_t - b x_t = u_t$ removes it
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Common trends} representation \refSW: $n$ variables with $r$ cointegrating vectors are driven by $n - r$ common stochastic trends
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $r = 0$: $n$ separate trends, no cointegration; $r = n - 1$: one trend shared by all
        \item example: three yields (1, 5 and 10 years) with $r = 2$ share one trend, the \textbf{level} of interest rates (Section 5)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Worked example}: $x_t$ a random walk, $y_t = 2x_t + u_t$, $z_t = -x_t + v_t$ ($u_t$, $v_t$ stationary)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $n = 3$, one common trend, so $r = 2$: e.g.\ $\beta_1 = (1, -2, 0)^\top$ and $\beta_2 = (0, 1, 2)^\top$ (since $y_t + 2z_t = u_t + 2v_t$)
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Where economics predicts cointegration}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Purchasing power parity}: $s_t = p_t - p^*_t + q_t$, with the real exchange rate $q_t$ stationary (Section 8)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $s_t$: log exchange rate (lei per euro); $p_t$, $p^*_t$: log price levels at home and abroad
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Term structure of interest rates}: by the expectations hypothesis, the spread between a long and a short yield is stationary \refCS
    \item \textbf{Consumption and income}: the ``great ratio'' $c_t - y_t$ (logs) is stable if consumption follows permanent income
    \item \textbf{Spot and futures prices}, an index and a fund that tracks it: arbitrage keeps the gap small
    \item \textbf{Shares of similar firms}: the same sector shocks; the basis of pairs trading (Section 9)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Four pairs of trending series}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_examples.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item US Treasury yields (FRED, monthly, since 1960); US real GDP and consumption (statsmodels macrodata, 1959--2009)
    \item Banca Transilvania and BRD (adjusted daily prices); EUR/RON and EUR/HUF (BNR reference rates, month-end)
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_common\_trends}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_common_trends}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the four pairs}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Each series is $I(1)$ (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}); the question is whether the two series of a pair move \textbf{together} in the long run
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Engle--Granger test (Section 2), 5\% critical value about $-3.34$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Yields: $\tau = -3.35$, p = 0.048: borderline; consumption and income: $\tau = -3.54$, p = 0.029
    \item The two banks: $\tau = -4.33$, p = 0.002: cointegrated in this sample
    \item EUR/RON and EUR/HUF: $\tau = -2.47$, p = 0.294: \textbf{not} cointegrated
    \begin{itemize}
        \item although they rose by similar amounts and $R^2 = 0.79$ in levels: a common direction is not a common trend
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Question for the room}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: two $I(1)$ series have a correlation of 0.95 in levels. Are they cointegrated?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: we cannot tell: unrelated random walks often have high correlations (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}); only a test on the equilibrium error decides
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: two cointegrated series have a correlation of 0.2 between their daily changes. Is this a contradiction?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: no: cointegration is about the long run; in the short run the changes can be almost unrelated
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: The idea of cointegration}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $I(1)$ series are cointegrated if a combination $\beta^\top \mathbf y_t$ is stationary: a long-run equilibrium
    \item Equivalently, they share common stochastic trends: $n$ variables, $r$ vectors, $n - r$ trends
    \item Theory suggests cointegration (parity conditions, spreads, great ratios), but the data must confirm it
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{The Engle--Granger two-step method}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Two steps}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Step 1}: estimate the long-run relation by OLS (ordinary least squares) in levels: $y_t = a + b\,x_t + u_t$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item keep the residuals $\hat u_t = y_t - \hat a - \hat b x_t$
        \item if the series are cointegrated, $\hat b$ is \textbf{super-consistent}: its error shrinks like $1/T$, faster than the usual $1/\sqrt{T}$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Step 2}: an ADF test (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}) on the residuals, without a constant: $\Delta\hat u_t = \gamma\,\hat u_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{k}\delta_j\Delta\hat u_{t-j} + e_t$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $H_0$: $\gamma = 0$, the residuals have a unit root: \textbf{no cointegration}; $H_1$: $\gamma < 0$: cointegration
        \item $\delta_j$: coefficients of the $k$ lagged differences, which absorb the autocorrelation of $\hat u_t$; $e_t$: white noise
        \item statistic $\tau = \hat\gamma/\mathrm{SE}(\hat\gamma)$, SE: standard error; reject $H_0$ when $\tau$ is below the critical value
    \end{itemize}
    \item Pretest: each series must be $I(1)$; cointegration between an $I(0)$ and an $I(1)$ series is impossible
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The reason the Dickey--Fuller table is wrong here}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item OLS chooses $\hat b$ to make the residual variance as small as possible
    \begin{itemize}
        \item so $\hat u_t$ looks more stationary than the true $u_t$, even when there is no cointegration
        \item under $H_0$ the statistic $\tau$ is shifted to the left of the Dickey--Fuller distribution
    \end{itemize}
    \item The critical values depend on the number of variables $n$ and on the deterministic terms of step 1
    \begin{itemize}
        \item tables: \refEG\ (by simulation), then \refMacKinnon\ and \refMacKinnonb, used by \texttt{statsmodels} (\texttt{coint})
    \end{itemize}
    \item With $\beta$ \textbf{known} from theory (e.g.\ a spread, $\beta = (1, -1)^\top$), nothing is estimated: the plain ADF test and its table apply
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The null distribution by simulation}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_eg_dist.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item 10\,000 samples of $T = 200$ independent Gaussian random walks; step 1 with a constant, step 2 without lags
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_engle\_granger}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_engle_granger}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the simulation: the critical values}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item 5\% quantiles: $-2.86$ (one series, Dickey--Fuller), $-3.33$ (2 variables), $-3.75$ (3 variables)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item MacKinnon's values for $T = 200$: $-2.88$; $-3.37$; $-3.78$: the simulation reproduces them
    \end{itemize}
    \item Using the Dickey--Fuller value $-2.88$ for the residuals would reject a true $H_0$ in 14.5\% of samples with 2 variables and 30.3\% with 3
    \begin{itemize}
        \item instead of 5\%: we would ``find'' cointegration far too often
    \end{itemize}
    \item More variables give OLS more freedom to fit, hence more negative critical values
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Critical values of the Engle--Granger test}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variables $n$} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{constant}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{constant and trend}} \\
 & 1\% & 5\% & 10\% & 1\% & 5\% & 10\% \\
\midrule
1 (Dickey--Fuller) & $-3.43$ & $-2.86$ & $-2.57$ & $-3.96$ & $-3.41$ & $-3.13$ \\
2 & $-3.90$ & $-3.34$ & $-3.04$ & $-4.33$ & $-3.78$ & $-3.50$ \\
3 & $-4.29$ & $-3.74$ & $-3.45$ & $-4.66$ & $-4.12$ & $-3.84$ \\
4 & $-4.64$ & $-4.10$ & $-3.81$ & $-4.97$ & $-4.43$ & $-4.15$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Asymptotic values ($T \to \infty$) of \refMacKinnonb; for finite $T$ the values are slightly more negative
    \item Read the row of the \textbf{total} number of variables in the regression, $y_t$ included
    \item Constant and trend in step 1: when the series have drifts that the relation does not cancel
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Phillips--Ouliaris test}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \refPO: the same step 1 and the same $H_0$ (no cointegration)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item step 2: a Dickey--Fuller regression \textbf{without} lagged differences; the $t$-statistic is corrected with the long-run variance of the residuals (as in the Phillips--Perron test of \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3})
        \item two versions: $Z_t$ (corrected $t$-ratio) and $Z_\alpha$ (corrected $T\hat\gamma$); the critical values of $Z_t$ are those of Engle--Granger
    \end{itemize}
    \item Reasons for two tests
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Engle--Granger depends on the number of lags $k$ chosen by AIC; Phillips--Ouliaris depends on the bandwidth of the long-run variance
        \item when they agree, the verdict is robust; when they disagree, look at the residual plot and at the sample
    \end{itemize}
    \item In Python: \texttt{coint(y, x)} from \texttt{statsmodels}; \texttt{phillips\_ouliaris(y, x, test\_type="Zt")} from \texttt{arch}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: US consumption and income}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Data: $c_t$, $y_t$ = 100 $\times$ log of real consumption and real GDP, quarterly, 1959Q1--2009Q3 (203 quarters)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item pretest: ADF with trend, p = 0.31 for $c_t$ and 0.39 for $y_t$: both $I(1)$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Step 1: $\hat c_t = -107.6 + 1.075\,y_t$, $R^2 = 0.9992$, DW $= 0.24$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item DW: the Durbin--Watson statistic of the residuals, about 2 without autocorrelation and close to 0 for very persistent residuals
        \item the slope is close to 1: a stable consumption share; but $R^2$ and DW alone prove nothing
    \end{itemize}
    \item Step 2: $\tau = -3.54$ with 0 lags; 5\% critical value for $n = 2$, $T = 203$: $-3.37$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $-3.54 < -3.37$: reject ``no cointegration'' at 5\% (p = 0.029); Phillips--Ouliaris: $Z_t = -3.52$, p = 0.031
        \item with the Dickey--Fuller value ($-2.88$) the decision would be the same here, but for the wrong reason
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The step-1 residuals}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.54\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_eg_steps.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Left and centre: $\hat u_t$ of consumption on income and of the 10-year on the 3-month Treasury yield; right: their sample ACF and that of a simulated random walk
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_engle\_granger}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_engle_granger}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the residuals}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Consumption: $\hat\rho(1) = 0.86$ but $\hat\rho(8) = 0.31$: deviations of 1--3\% that shrink markedly within about two years
    \item Yields: $\hat\rho(1) = 0.97$, $\hat\rho(12) = 0.58$: very persistent deviations; a borderline test ($\tau = -3.35$, p = 0.048)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item high persistence is the usual situation: the power of the test against $\rho$ close to 1 is low (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3})
    \end{itemize}
    \item A random walk decays much more slowly: the ACF alone cannot settle the question; the test can
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Engle--Granger and Phillips--Ouliaris on real data}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{llrrrrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Regression} & \textbf{Freq.} & $T$ & $\hat b$ & $\tau$ (k) & p & $Z_t$ & p \\
\midrule
US consumption on income & quarterly & 203 & 1.07 & $-3.54$ (0) & 0.029 & $-3.52$ & 0.031 \\
US: 10-year on 3-month yield & monthly & 801 & 0.86 & $-3.35$ (20) & 0.048 & $-4.04$ & 0.006 \\
TLV on BRD (since 2014) & daily & 3\,176 & 1.36 & $-4.33$ (3) & 0.002 & $-4.14$ & 0.005 \\
BRD on TLV (since 2014) & daily & 3\,176 & 0.71 & $-4.16$ (3) & 0.004 & $-4.02$ & 0.007 \\
TLV on BRD (since 2010) & daily & 4\,187 & 1.68 & $-1.82$ (3) & 0.622 & $-1.83$ & 0.619 \\
EUR/RON on EUR/HUF & monthly & 255 & 0.71 & $-2.47$ (0) & 0.294 & $-2.43$ & 0.309 \\
Romania: consumption on GDP & quarterly & 126 & 1.46 & $-2.32$ (8) & 0.363 & $-6.80$ & $<$\,0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\tau$: Engle--Granger statistic ($k$ lags by AIC); p-values of \refMacKinnonb\ for 2 variables; $Z_t$: Phillips--Ouliaris
    \item Banks: adjusted prices from data/market; Romania: household consumption and GDP, Eurostat, chain-linked volumes, seasonally adjusted, since 1995
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the table}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Normalisation}: TLV on BRD and BRD on TLV give different $\tau$ ($-4.33$ and $-4.16$) and slopes that are not exact inverses
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Engle--Granger depends on which variable is on the left; here the verdict is the same
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{The sample}: since 2010 the same banks are not cointegrated (p = 0.622); since 2014 they are (p = 0.002)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item choosing the start date after looking at the data is a form of data snooping
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{The two tests disagree} for Romania: Engle--Granger p = 0.363 with 8 lags, Phillips--Ouliaris p $<$\,0.001
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the slope 1.46 is far from 1: the consumption share rose strongly; Seminar 7 (B2) discusses this case
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Limits of the Engle--Granger method}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{At most one} cointegrating vector: with $n \ge 3$ variables there may be several (Sections 4--5)
    \item \textbf{Normalisation}: the results depend on the variable put on the left
    \item \textbf{Inference on $\hat b$}: super-consistent, but biased in small samples, and its OLS $t$-statistics are \textbf{not} valid
    \begin{itemize}
        \item remedy: dynamic OLS (DOLS) \refSWd, adding leads and lags of $\Delta x_t$, gives valid standard errors
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Two-step errors}: mistakes in step 1 carry over to step 2; the power is low against slow adjustment
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the Johansen method (Section 5) estimates everything at once, by maximum likelihood
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Case study: Engle and Granger (1987)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.30\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.44\textheight]{ch7_robert_engle_2022.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Robert Engle (2022); Nobel Prize in Economics 2003}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:0603_KRBN-RobertEngle-JonDemske-10.jpg}{Photo: Jon Demske (2022); CC BY-SA 4.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.66\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: how to model $I(1)$ series that are tied in the long run, without spurious regressions and without differencing away the long run?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \refEG, written at the University of California, San Diego, one of the most cited papers in econometrics
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Contribution}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the definition of cointegration and the representation theorem (Section 4): cointegration $\Leftrightarrow$ error correction
        \item the two-step estimator and residual-based tests with simulated critical values
        \item applications to US series such as consumption and income, prices and wages, short and long interest rates
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Recognition}: Nobel Prize 2003, Granger for cointegration, Engle for ARCH (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter5_conditional_volatility_garch.pdf}{Chapter 5})
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: The Engle--Granger method}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Step 1: OLS in levels (super-consistent $\hat b$); step 2: ADF on the residuals, $H_0$: no cointegration
    \item Critical values of Engle--Granger (MacKinnon), more negative than Dickey--Fuller and dependent on $n$
    \item Check with Phillips--Ouliaris, with the reverse normalisation and with another sample
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Error correction models}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The error correction model}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item With $u_{t-1} = y_{t-1} - a - b x_{t-1}$ (last period's equilibrium error), the \textbf{error correction model} (ECM) is
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\Delta y_t = c + \gamma\,u_{t-1} + \delta_0\,\Delta x_t + \sum_{j \ge 1}(\phi_j\Delta y_{t-j} + \delta_j\Delta x_{t-j}) + \varepsilon_t$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Every term is stationary: OLS and the usual $t$-tests are valid (with $\hat u_{t-1}$ from step 1)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $b$: the \textbf{long-run} effect of $x$ on $y$; $\delta_0$: the \textbf{short-run} (same-period) effect
        \item $\gamma$: the \textbf{speed of adjustment}; error correction requires $-2 < \gamma < 0$
        \item $c$: constant; $\phi_j$, $\delta_j$: short-run coefficients of the lagged differences; $\varepsilon_t$: white noise
    \end{itemize}
    \item Reading: if $y_{t-1}$ was above equilibrium ($u_{t-1} > 0$) and $\gamma < 0$, then $y_t$ tends to fall: a share $|\gamma|$ of the gap is closed each period
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Speed of adjustment and half-life}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Without new shocks, the equilibrium error evolves as $u_t = (1 + \gamma)\,u_{t-1}$, so $u_h = (1 + \gamma)^h u_0$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item (in a bivariate system where only $y$ adjusts)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Half-life}: the number of periods after which half of a deviation is gone
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $(1 + \gamma)^{h} = 0.5 \;\Rightarrow\; h_{1/2} = \ln 0.5 / \ln(1 + \gamma)$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Worked example}: $\gamma = -0.2$, $h_{1/2} = \ln 0.5/\ln 0.8 = 3.1$ periods
    \begin{itemize}
        \item in months: about three months for half of a deviation; in quarters: three quarters
    \end{itemize}
    \item Compare half-lives only in the same time unit: a monthly and a quarterly $\gamma$ are not comparable
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Half-lives: theory and estimates}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_ecm.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Left: $(1 + \gamma)^h$ for three speeds; right: the decay implied by the estimated ECMs of US consumption (quarters) and of the 10-year yield (months)
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_error\_correction}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_error_correction}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the estimated ECMs}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Consumption: $\hat\gamma = -0.047$ ($t = -1.75$), half-life 14.3 quarters; $\hat\delta_0 = 0.54$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item half of a rise in income reaches consumption in the same quarter; the rest comes slowly, and the adjustment term is only marginally significant
    \end{itemize}
    \item 10-year yield: $\hat\gamma = -0.033$ ($t = -4.94$), half-life 20.8 months; $\hat\delta_0 = 0.38$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the 3-month rate also reacts to the same gap: $\hat\gamma = 0.024$ ($t = 2.08$), with the opposite sign: both rates move towards each other
    \end{itemize}
    \item When both variables adjust, a single-equation ECM tells only half of the story: hence the VECM (Section 4)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: one quarter of consumption}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Estimated ECM (main terms): $\Delta c_t = 0.418 + 0.54\,\Delta y_t -0.047\,\hat u_{t-1} + \dots$, with $\hat u_{t-1} = c_{t-1} - 1.075\,y_{t-1} - \hat a$
    \item Scenario: consumption is $2\%$ above its equilibrium ($\hat u_{t-1} = 2$) and income grows by $1\%$ this quarter
    \begin{itemize}
        \item short-run effect: $0.537 \times 1 = 0.537$; error correction: $-0.047 \times 2 = -0.095$
        \item predicted growth of consumption: about $0.86\%$ (the lagged differences are set to 0)
    \end{itemize}
    \item Without the error correction term, the model would ignore that consumption is already too high
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Case study: the consumption function of DHSY (1978)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: why did the consumption functions of the 1970s, estimated in levels or in differences, forecast UK consumers' expenditure so badly?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \refDHSY\ (Davidson, Hendry, Srba and Yeo, ``DHSY''): quarterly UK data on expenditure and income
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Method}: a model in differences plus the lagged log ratio of expenditure to income, the error correction term
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a general-to-specific search, starting from a large dynamic model
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Legacy}: the ECM form came first; \refGranger\ and \refEG\ then showed why it works: the two series are cointegrated
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a test of cointegration can also use the $t$-statistic of $\gamma$ in the ECM, with its own critical values \refBDM
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Error correction models}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item ECM: $\Delta y_t$ on $\Delta x_t$, lagged differences and $\hat u_{t-1}$; all terms stationary
    \item $\gamma < 0$: speed of adjustment; half-life $\ln 0.5/\ln(1 + \gamma)$, in the units of the data
    \item Short run ($\delta_0$) and long run ($b$) in one equation; if several variables adjust, we need a system
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{The VECM and the Granger representation theorem}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{From a VAR to a VECM}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6}: a VAR($p$) in levels, $\mathbf y_t = \mathbf c + A_1\mathbf y_{t-1} + \dots + A_p\mathbf y_{t-p} + \mathbf u_t$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item subtract $\mathbf y_{t-1}$ and regroup the lags: the same model in \textbf{vector error correction} form (VECM)
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\Delta\mathbf y_t = \mathbf c + \Pi\,\mathbf y_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\Gamma_i\,\Delta\mathbf y_{t-i} + \mathbf u_t$, \quad $\Pi = A_1 + \dots + A_p - I$, \quad $\Gamma_i = -(A_{i+1} + \dots + A_p)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\Pi$: the long-run matrix (it multiplies the levels); $\Gamma_i$: the short-run matrices; $I$: the identity matrix
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Derivation} for $p = 2$: $\mathbf y_t - \mathbf y_{t-1} = (A_1 - I)\mathbf y_{t-1} + A_2\mathbf y_{t-2} + \mathbf u_t$; add and subtract $A_2\mathbf y_{t-1}$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\Delta\mathbf y_t = (A_1 + A_2 - I)\,\mathbf y_{t-1} - A_2\,\Delta\mathbf y_{t-1} + \mathbf u_t$: $\Pi = A_1 + A_2 - I$, $\Gamma_1 = -A_2$
    \end{itemize}
    \item The VECM is a rewriting, not a new model: all the information about the long run sits in the matrix $\Pi$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The rank of $\Pi$}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\Delta\mathbf y_t$ is stationary; so $\Pi\mathbf y_{t-1}$ must be stationary too. Three cases, by $r = \mathrm{rank}(\Pi)$:
    \item $r = 0$: $\Pi = 0$; no cointegration; the right model is a \textbf{VAR in differences}
    \item $r = n$: $\Pi$ has full rank; $\mathbf y_t$ is already stationary; a \textbf{VAR in levels} (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6})
    \item $0 < r < n$: \textbf{cointegration} with $r$ vectors; $\Pi = \alpha\beta^\top$ with $\alpha$, $\beta$ of size $n \times r$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\beta^\top\mathbf y_{t-1}$: the $r$ equilibrium errors; $\alpha$: the \textbf{adjustment coefficients} (loadings), how strongly each variable reacts to each error
        \item only the product is unique: $\alpha\beta^\top = (\alpha Q)(\beta Q^{-\top})^\top$ for any invertible $Q$; we normalise $\beta$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Testing for cointegration = testing the rank of $\Pi$ (Section 5)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Granger representation theorem}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Theorem} \refEG: if $\mathbf y_t$ is $I(1)$ and cointegrated with rank $r$, then it has a VECM representation with $\Pi = \alpha\beta^\top$, and conversely
    \begin{itemize}
        \item cointegration $\Leftrightarrow$ error correction: the equilibrium error must feed back into the changes
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Consequences}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a VAR in differences omits $\alpha\beta^\top\mathbf y_{t-1}$: it is \textbf{misspecified} when the series are cointegrated
        \item $\alpha \neq 0$: at least one variable adjusts, so there is Granger causality (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6}) in at least one direction
        \item the levels are driven by $n - r$ common stochastic trends; the effects of shocks on the levels do not die out
    \end{itemize}
    \item A VAR in levels is not wrong either: it is consistent, but it ignores the restriction $\mathrm{rank}(\Pi) = r$ and its tests are non-standard
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{2003: the Nobel Prize for cointegration}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.34\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.40\textheight]{ch3_clive_granger_2008.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Clive Granger (1934--2009)}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Clive_Granger_by_Olaf_Storbeck_(3x4_cropped).jpg}{Photo: Olaf Storbeck (2008); CC BY-SA 2.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.62\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.30\textheight]{ch7_granger_building_2012.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{The Sir Clive Granger Building, University of Nottingham}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:University_Park_MMB_\%C2\%AB24_Sir_Clive_Granger_Building.jpg}{Photo: mattbuck (2012); CC BY-SA 3.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Granger studied and began his career at Nottingham; cointegration was developed at UC San Diego
    \item Nobel lecture: \refGrangerN: ``time series analysis, cointegration, and applications''
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: a bivariate VECM}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\Delta y_{1t} = -0.10\,(y_{1,t-1} - y_{2,t-1}) + u_{1t}$, \quad $\Delta y_{2t} = 0.10\,(y_{1,t-1} - y_{2,t-1}) + u_{2t}$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\beta = (1, -1)^\top$, $\alpha = (-0.10, 0.10)^\top$; $\Pi = \alpha\beta^\top = \begin{pmatrix} -0.10 & 0.10 \\ 0.10 & -0.10 \end{pmatrix}$, $\det\Pi = 0$, rank 1
    \end{itemize}
    \item If $y_1$ is above $y_2$: $y_1$ falls ($\alpha_1 < 0$) and $y_2$ rises ($\alpha_2 > 0$): both close the gap
    \item The gap $z_t = y_{1t} - y_{2t}$: $z_t = (1 + \beta^\top\alpha)\,z_{t-1} + (u_{1t} - u_{2t}) = 0.8\,z_{t-1} + \dots$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a stationary AR(1); half-life $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.8 = 3.1$ periods; the condition is $-2 < \beta^\top\alpha < 0$
    \end{itemize}
    \item The average $(y_{1t} + y_{2t})/2$ changes by $(u_{1t} + u_{2t})/2$: a random walk, the common trend
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Deterministic terms: five cases}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.4cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.6cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Case} & \textbf{In the VECM} & \textbf{Implication for the data} & \texttt{statsmodels} \\
\midrule
1 & no constant, no trend & no drift; relations through the origin & \texttt{n} \\
2 & constant only inside $\beta^\top\mathbf y_{t-1}$ & no drift; equilibrium errors with a non-zero mean (yields, spreads) & \texttt{ci} \\
3 & unrestricted constant & linear trends in the levels, none in the relations (GDP, prices) & \texttt{co} \\
4 & constant, and a trend inside $\beta^\top\mathbf y_{t-1}$ & trends in the levels and in the relations & \texttt{coli} \\
5 & unrestricted constant and trend & quadratic trends in the levels; rarely plausible & \texttt{colo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item The critical values of the Johansen tests change with the case \refJohBook; choose the case from the plot and from theory, before testing
    \item \texttt{coint\_johansen} of \texttt{statsmodels} implements case 1 (\texttt{det\_order=-1}) and case 3 (\texttt{det\_order=0}), the case used in this chapter
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Weak exogeneity}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item If a row of $\alpha$ is zero, $\alpha_i = 0$, the variable $y_i$ does \textbf{not} react to the equilibrium errors
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $y_i$ is \textbf{weakly exogenous} for $\beta$: the other variables do all the adjusting
        \item $y_i$ pushes the common trend; e.g.\ Euribor for Romanian interest rates (Seminar 7, B4)
    \end{itemize}
    \item Test: a $t$-test on $\alpha_i$ (one cointegrating vector) or a likelihood-ratio (LR) test of $\alpha_i = 0$ \refJohB
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the statistic is asymptotically $\chi^2$ with $r$ degrees of freedom, once $r$ is fixed
    \end{itemize}
    \item Use: if $x_t$ is weakly exogenous, a single-equation ECM for $y_t$ (Section 3) loses no information about $\beta$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: The VECM}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\Delta\mathbf y_t = \alpha\beta^\top\mathbf y_{t-1} + \sum\Gamma_i\Delta\mathbf y_{t-i} + \mathbf u_t$: a VAR rewritten; $\mathrm{rank}(\Pi) = r$
    \item Granger representation: cointegration $\Leftrightarrow$ error correction; a VAR in differences omits the long run
    \item $\beta$: equilibria; $\alpha$: who adjusts; deterministic terms: five cases; $\alpha_i = 0$: weak exogeneity
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{The Johansen tests}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The idea: reduced-rank regression}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.36\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.36\textheight]{ch7_copenhagen_university_2011.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{University of Copenhagen, where Søren Johansen and Katarina Juselius developed the method}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Copenhagen_University_Main_Entrance_DSC09700.jpg}{Photo: Per Meistrup (2011); CC BY-SA 4.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.60\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \refJohA, \refJohB: maximum likelihood for the VECM with Gaussian errors
    \begin{itemize}
        \item regress $\Delta\mathbf y_t$ and $\mathbf y_{t-1}$ on the lagged differences; keep the residuals $R_{0t}$ and $R_{1t}$
        \item find the combinations of $R_{1t}$ most correlated with $R_{0t}$: the \textbf{canonical correlations}
    \end{itemize}
    \item Their squares are the eigenvalues $1 > \hat\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \hat\lambda_n \ge 0$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a large $\hat\lambda_i$: a stationary combination that predicts the changes; $\hat\lambda_i \approx 0$: a combination that is still $I(1)$
        \item the eigenvectors give $\hat\beta$; then $\hat\alpha$ follows by OLS
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Trace and maximum-eigenvalue statistics}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Trace test}: $H_0$: rank $\le r$, against rank $= n$; \quad $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(r) = -T\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\ln(1 - \hat\lambda_i)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item it sums the information in the $n - r$ smallest eigenvalues: if they are all close to 0, the statistic is small and $H_0$ is kept
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Maximum-eigenvalue test}: $H_0$: rank $= r$, against rank $= r + 1$; \quad $\lambda_{\max}(r) = -T\ln(1 - \hat\lambda_{r+1})$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item it uses only the next eigenvalue, $\hat\lambda_{r+1}$; $T$: the number of observations
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Sequential procedure}: test $r = 0$, then $r \le 1$, \dots; the rank is the first $r$ whose $H_0$ is \textbf{not} rejected
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the statistics are likelihood ratios, but their distributions are non-standard (functions of Brownian motions)
        \item critical values depend on $n - r$ and on the deterministic case: \refOL, \refMHM
    \end{itemize}
    \item The two tests usually agree; if not, the trace test is preferred in most applied work
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: from eigenvalues to statistics}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item US yields at 1, 5 and 10 years, monthly, $T = 801$: $\hat\lambda = (0.0405, 0.0229, 0.0039)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $-\ln(1 - \hat\lambda_i)$: 0.0414; 0.0231; 0.0039
    \end{itemize}
    \item $r = 0$: trace $= 801 \times (0.0414 + 0.0231 + 0.0039) = 54.8 > 29.80$: reject
    \begin{itemize}
        \item max-eigenvalue: $801 \times 0.0414 = 33.2 > 21.13$: reject
    \end{itemize}
    \item $r \le 1$: trace $= 21.7 > 15.49$: reject; \quad $r \le 2$: trace $= 3.1 < 3.84$: do not reject
    \begin{itemize}
        \item rank 2: two cointegrating vectors, one common trend
    \end{itemize}
    \item Small eigenvalues still matter: they are multiplied by $T$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Johansen tests on three systems}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{lrrcccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{System} & $T$ & $k$ & $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(0)$ & $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(1)$ & $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(2)$ & $\lambda_{\max}(0)$ & $\lambda_{\max}(1)$ & \textbf{rank} \\
\midrule
US yields 1y, 5y, 10y & 801 & 2 & 54.6 & 21.6 & 3.1 & 33.0 & 18.5 & 2 \\
US output, consumption, investment & 203 & 1 & 28.9 & 11.4 & 2.6 & 17.4 & 8.9 & 0 \\
EUR/RON, EUR/HUF, EUR/PLN & 255 & 1 & 24.2 & 7.9 & 2.7 & 16.3 & 5.2 & 0 \\
5\% critical value & & & 29.80 & 15.49 & 3.84 & 21.13 & 14.26 & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Case 3 (unrestricted constant); $k$: lagged differences chosen by BIC on the VAR in levels; ranks by the trace test (the maximum-eigenvalue test gives the same ranks here)
    \item Yields: FRED, 1960--2026; output, consumption and investment: 100 ln, US 1959--2009; currencies: BNR, month-end, 2005--2026
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the three systems}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Yields: rank 2, so one common trend: the \textbf{level} of rates moves all maturities; the two spreads are stationary
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the expectations hypothesis of the term structure \refCS\ in its weak form
    \end{itemize}
    \item Output, consumption and investment: trace 28.9 against 29.80: rank 0 at 5\%, a near miss
    \begin{itemize}
        \item balanced growth predicts rank 2 (stable shares of consumption and investment); with Engle--Granger, consumption and income were cointegrated (p = 0.029): low power, not proof of absence
    \end{itemize}
    \item Currencies: trace 24.2: rank 0; three separate stochastic trends (Section 8)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The deterministic case changes the answer}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Deterministic terms} & $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(0)$ & 5\% & $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(1)$ & 5\% & $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(2)$ & 5\% \\
\midrule
none (\texttt{det\_order=-1}) & 45.9 & 24.28 & 13.3 & 12.32 & 0.4 & 4.13 \\
constant (\texttt{det\_order=0}) & 54.6 & 29.80 & 21.6 & 15.49 & 3.1 & 3.84 \\
linear trend (\texttt{det\_order=1}) & 60.0 & 35.01 & 23.7 & 18.40 & 4.8 & 3.84 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item US yields at 1, 5 and 10 years: ranks 2, 2 and 3
    \item With a linear trend, the test says that every yield is stationary around a trend: not plausible for interest rates over 66 years
    \begin{itemize}
        \item choose the deterministic terms from theory and from the plot, not from the result you like
    \end{itemize}
    \item Other practical issues: the lag length $k$; size distortions in small samples (correction factor $(T - nk)/T$, \refRA); structural breaks
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Case study: Johansen and Juselius (1990)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: is there a stable demand for money in Denmark and Finland?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \refJJ: real money, real income, interest rates (and inflation); quarterly data
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Method}: the VECM by maximum likelihood; the rank by the trace and maximum-eigenvalue tests; then \textbf{tests of restrictions} on $\beta$ and $\alpha$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item e.g.\ a unit income elasticity, $\beta = (1, -1, \cdot)$; weak exogeneity of income and interest rates
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Legacy}: the template of the ``cointegrated VAR'' methodology \refJus: test the rank, then test economic hypotheses as restrictions
    \begin{itemize}
        \item one of the most cited papers in applied econometrics
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: The Johansen tests}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Eigenvalues of a reduced-rank regression; trace and maximum-eigenvalue statistics; sequential testing from $r = 0$
    \item Critical values depend on $n - r$ and on the deterministic case
    \item Yields: rank 2; macro aggregates: borderline; currencies: rank 0
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Estimating and interpreting $\beta$ and $\alpha$}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The term-structure VECM}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_rates.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item US Treasury yields at 1, 5 and 10 years (FRED GS1, GS5, GS10), January 1960--September 2026; VECM with rank 2, 2 lagged differences, constant restricted to the relations (case 2)
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_johansen\_vecm}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_johansen_vecm}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the cointegrating vectors}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Normalisation on the 1-year and 5-year yields: $\hat\beta_1^\top\mathbf y_t = i^{(1)}_t - 1.045\,i^{(10)}_t + 1.22$, $\hat\beta_2^\top\mathbf y_t = i^{(5)}_t - 1.044\,i^{(10)}_t + 0.59$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item both slopes close to 1: the equilibria are almost the spreads $i^{(1)} - i^{(10)}$ and $i^{(5)} - i^{(10)}$, with mean term premia
    \end{itemize}
    \item The equilibrium errors are stationary: ADF p $<$\,0.001 and 0.008; they are large in the 1980s and around zero-rate periods
    \item A formal test of $\beta = (1, -1)$ for each spread is a likelihood-ratio test \refJohB; with super-consistent $\hat\beta$, values this close to 1 are informative
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The adjustment coefficients}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Equation} & $\hat\alpha_{\cdot 1}$ & $t$ & $\hat\alpha_{\cdot 2}$ & $t$ \\
\midrule
$\Delta i^{(1)}_t$ (1 year) & $-0.021$ & $-0.82$ & $0.024$ & $0.31$ \\
$\Delta i^{(5)}_t$ (5 years) & $0.045$ & $2.21$ & $-0.122$ & $-2.00$ \\
$\Delta i^{(10)}_t$ (10 years) & $0.040$ & $2.22$ & $-0.077$ & $-1.43$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item The 1-year yield does not react to either error ($|t| < 1$): it behaves as \textbf{weakly exogenous}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the short end follows monetary policy; the 5- and 10-year yields do the adjusting ($|t| \approx 2$)
    \end{itemize}
    \item The equilibrium errors $\mathbf z_t = \hat\beta^\top\mathbf y_t$ follow $\mathbf z_t = (I + \hat\beta^\top\hat\alpha)\,\mathbf z_{t-1} + \dots$; eigenvalues 0.969 and 0.926
    \begin{itemize}
        \item half-lives of about 22.1 and 9.0 months: slow error correction, typical of interest rates
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Impulse responses of the VECM}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.50\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_vecm_irf.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Orthogonalised responses (Cholesky, ordering 1y, 5y, 10y; \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6}) to a one-standard-deviation shock to the 1-year yield
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_johansen\_vecm}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_johansen_vecm}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the impulse responses}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item On impact: +0.36, +0.24 and +0.19 percentage points for 1, 5 and 10 years
    \begin{itemize}
        \item after 60 months: +0.37, +0.36 and +0.33: the effects do \textbf{not} die out and become almost equal
    \end{itemize}
    \item A permanent shift of the common trend (the level), with stationary spreads: the signature of $n - r = 1$ common trend
    \item In a stationary VAR (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6}) every response returns to zero; in a VECM the long-run responses are generally different from zero
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: $\beta$ and $\alpha$}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\hat\beta$: normalise, read as equilibria (spreads, ratios), test economic restrictions
    \item $\hat\alpha$: who adjusts and how fast; a zero row means weak exogeneity
    \item Shocks have permanent effects on cointegrated levels, but not on the equilibrium errors
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Forecasting: VECM or VAR in differences?}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The theoretical arguments}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item VECM forecasts keep the equilibria: as the horizon grows, $\hat\beta^\top\hat{\mathbf y}_{T+h}$ returns to its mean
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a VAR in differences forgets the levels: its forecasts of the spreads stay where they are
    \end{itemize}
    \item \refEY: imposing cointegration improves long-horizon forecasts in simulated systems
    \item \refCD: the gains are concentrated in the \textbf{cointegrating combinations}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item for the individual levels, the forecast error is dominated by the common trend, which no model can predict
        \item estimation error in $\alpha$, $\beta$ and in the constants can make a VECM worse in practice
    \end{itemize}
    \item Test it out of sample, with re-estimation at each forecast origin
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The forecasting experiment}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Data: US yields at 1, 5 and 10 years, monthly, since 1960
    \item 135 forecast origins, every three months from January 1990 to July 2023; models re-estimated on the data up to each origin
    \begin{itemize}
        \item VECM with rank 2 and a restricted constant; VAR in differences without constant, with the same lags; random walk (no change)
    \end{itemize}
    \item Horizons of 1 to 36 months; RMSE (root mean squared error) of each model divided by that of the random walk
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ratio below 1: better than the random walk; also for the 10-year minus 1-year spread
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{VECM against a VAR in differences, out of sample}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.52\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_forecast.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item RMSE relative to the random walk by horizon; first three panels: the yields; last panel: the 10-year minus 1-year spread
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_forecasting}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_forecasting}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the forecast comparison}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Levels: neither model beats the random walk clearly; the VECM is worse at short horizons (1 year at 6 months: 1.14; 5 years: 1.06)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the VAR in differences stays close to 1 at every horizon (1 year at 12 months: 1.00)
    \end{itemize}
    \item Spread: the VECM gains at long horizons: 0.85 at 24 months and 0.74 at 36 months; the VAR in differences: 1.00
    \begin{itemize}
        \item exactly the pattern of \refCD: cointegration helps forecast the equilibrium errors, not the trend
    \end{itemize}
    \item Lesson: use a VECM when the object of interest is the relation (a spread, a ratio, a pair); for the levels alone, a random walk is hard to beat
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Forecasting}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item The VECM pulls the forecasts of the equilibrium errors back to their means; the VAR in differences does not
    \item Out of sample: gains for the spread at long horizons, none for the levels
    \item Always compare with the random walk, with re-estimation and without look-ahead
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Economic examples: parity and interest rates}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Purchasing power parity}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.34\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.34\textheight]{ch7_bnr_palace_2015.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{The National Bank of Romania, which publishes the reference rates}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bucharest_-_BNR_Palace_(19644434340).jpg}{Photo: Ștefan Jurcă (2015); CC BY 2.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.62\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Relative PPP} (purchasing power parity): the exchange rate offsets inflation differences
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $s_t = 100\ln(\mathrm{EUR/RON})$; $p_t$, $p^*_t$: $100\ln$ of the HICP (Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices) of Romania and of the euro area
        \item PPP holds in the long run if the real exchange rate $q_t = s_t - p_t + p^*_t$ is stationary: cointegration with $\beta = (1, -1, 1)$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Reasons why it may fail
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \refBalassa: fast productivity growth in tradables raises prices of non-tradables in a catching-up economy: a trend real appreciation
        \item even where PPP holds, deviations decay slowly; the survey \refTT\ reports half-lives of several years
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{PPP for the leu}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_ppp.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Monthly, July 2005--August 2026: EUR/RON (monthly mean of the BNR reference rate), HICP of Romania and of the euro area (Eurostat, 2015 = 100)
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_parity\_conditions}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_parity_conditions}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting PPP for the leu}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Since 2005 the leu lost 38.7 log points against the euro, while Romanian prices rose 52.4 log points more than euro-area prices
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the real exchange rate changed by $-13.7$ log points: a real appreciation of the leu, concentrated after 2021
    \end{itemize}
    \item ADF on $q_t$: p = 0.24; Engle--Granger of $s_t$ on $p_t - p^*_t$: slope 0.89, p = 0.34; Johansen on $(s_t, p_t, p^*_t)$: rank 0
    \item No evidence of PPP over 21 years, consistent with Balassa--Samuelson convergence; 21 years may also be too short for half-lives of several years
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{ROBOR and Euribor}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_ro_ea_rates.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Three-month money market rates (Eurostat), August 1995--August 2026: ROBOR 3M for Romania and Euribor 3M for the euro area
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_parity\_conditions}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_parity_conditions}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting ROBOR and Euribor}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Full sample: Engle--Granger p = 0.52, Phillips--Ouliaris p = 0.010: the disinflation of the 1990s dominates and the tests disagree
    \item Since 2010: p = 0.047 (Engle--Granger) and 0.029 (Phillips--Ouliaris), slope 1.19, mean spread 3.11 percentage points
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ECM for ROBOR: $\hat\gamma = -0.020$ ($t = -1.18$), half-life about 34 months: weak and slow adjustment
    \end{itemize}
    \item Romanian monetary policy follows its own inflation target; the link to Euribor is loose (Seminar 7, B4, adds the Romanian 10-year yield)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Three Central European currencies}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_cee_fx.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item EUR/RON, EUR/HUF and EUR/PLN, cross rates from the BNR reference rates, month-end, 100 ln
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_parity\_conditions}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_parity_conditions}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the three currencies}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Since July 2005: EUR/RON +40.1, EUR/HUF +39.5, EUR/PLN +6.7 log points; each rate is $I(1)$ (ADF p = 0.55; 0.75; 0.08)
    \item Johansen: trace 24.2 for $r = 0$ (critical value 29.80); also no cointegration since 2012 (trace 12.7)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a common anchor (the euro) and similar shocks do not create a common trend: each central bank and each inflation path adds its own
    \end{itemize}
    \item The right model for these rates is a VAR in differences (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6}); Seminar 7 (B3) repeats the analysis
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Economic examples}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item PPP for the leu is rejected over 2005--2026: real appreciation of a converging economy
    \item ROBOR and Euribor: a loose, slow link since 2010; the sample decides the verdict
    \item Theory proposes $\beta$; the tests, the sample and the deterministic terms decide whether the data agree
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{An application: pairs trading}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The idea of pairs trading}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Two shares exposed to the same shocks (two banks, two oil companies) may be cointegrated: their spread mean-reverts
    \begin{itemize}
        \item when the spread is unusually wide, sell the expensive share and buy the cheap one; close when the spread is back
    \end{itemize}
    \item A \textbf{relative-value} trade: the market direction cancels out; the profit comes from the error correction
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \refGGR: the distance method on US shares, profitable over 1962--2002
        \item \refDoFaff: the profits declined in later years
    \end{itemize}
    \item A good test of a time-series idea: it must work \textbf{out of sample}, \textbf{after costs}, and on pairs chosen \textbf{without looking ahead}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A rule without look-ahead}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Formation} (the previous 252 trading days): test every pair with Engle--Granger; keep the pairs with p $<$ 0.05
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $P_{A,t}$, $P_{B,t}$: the prices of shares A and B; $r_A$, $r_B$: their daily log returns
        \item hedge ratio $\hat b$ by OLS of $\ln P_A$ on $\ln P_B$; mean $\bar s$ and standard deviation $\hat\sigma_s$ of the spread $s_t = \ln P_{A,t} - \hat a - \hat b\ln P_{B,t}$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Trading} (the next 126 days), with the formation parameters fixed: $z_t = (s_t - \bar s)/\hat\sigma_s$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $z_t > 2$: short A, long $\hat b$ of B; $z_t < -2$: the opposite; close at $z_t = 0$ or at the end of the window
        \item daily return per unit of gross exposure: $\pm(r_A - \hat b\,r_B)/(1 + |\hat b|)$; equal capital per selected pair
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Costs}: 0.20\% (Bucharest) and 0.05\% (US) of the gross exposure traded, at each opening and closing
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Banca Transilvania and BRD}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_pair.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Adjusted daily prices since 2014; right: the spread of the full-sample regression, standardised, with the entry bands
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_pairs\_trading}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_pairs_trading}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the bank pair}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Full sample: $\hat b = 1.36$; the spread is an AR(1) with $\hat\rho = 0.990$: half-life about 69 trading days
    \begin{itemize}
        \item only 5.0\% of the days lie outside $\pm 2$: few trading opportunities, each lasting months
    \end{itemize}
    \item Trading this picture with full-sample parameters gives 3.32\% per year (Sharpe ratio 0.44), after costs
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Sharpe ratio: the mean annual return divided by the annual standard deviation of the returns
        \item an illusion: $\hat b$, $\bar s$ and $\hat\sigma_s$ use the future, and the pair was chosen because it looks cointegrated since 2014
    \end{itemize}
    \item With the rolling rule, the pair passes the formation test in none of its 24 windows: one year of data is too short to detect such slow error correction
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Pairs trading out of sample}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch7_pairs_backtest.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Left: 8 liquid BVB shares (TLV, BRD, SNP, TGN, TEL, EL, SNG, SNN), since 2015; right: 6 US banks (JPM, BAC, C, WFC, GS, MS), since 2005
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch7\_pairs\_trading}{\qlurl{TSA_ch7_pairs_trading}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the backtest}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Bucharest: 22 windows, pairs found in 14, 73 trades, 62\% of trades profitable, but the mean return per trade is $-0.26$\%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item gross 1.17\% per year (Sharpe 0.15); net 0.41\% (Sharpe 0.05); break-even cost 0.31\%
    \end{itemize}
    \item US banks: gross 2.77\% (Sharpe 0.16), net 2.57\% (Sharpe 0.14), 80 trades
    \begin{itemize}
        \item with a deep loss in the autumn of 2008: cointegration can break exactly when it matters
    \end{itemize}
    \item Many small wins and a few large losses: the typical profile of a mean-reversion strategy
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Pitfalls of pairs trading}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Multiple testing}: with 28 pairs and a 5\% test, about 1.4 pairs pass by chance in each window
    \item \textbf{Look-ahead}: choosing pairs, start dates or thresholds after seeing the whole sample
    \item \textbf{Breaks}: mergers, recapitalisations, regulation and crises change $\beta$; the spread may never come back
    \item \textbf{Market frictions}: short selling is limited on the BVB, borrowing shares costs a fee, bid-ask spreads are wide for small caps
    \item \textbf{Slow error correction}: half-lives of months mean capital tied up for months, and a long wait in a losing position
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Pairs trading}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Pairs trading bets on error correction in the spread of two cointegrated shares
    \item In sample it looks attractive; out of sample, after costs, the profits on the BVB are close to zero
    \item Report the selection, the costs, the number of trades and the worst episode, not only the Sharpe ratio
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Possible contribution of AI}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Possible contribution of AI}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Code}: a first draft of a script that runs unit-root tests, Engle--Granger, Phillips--Ouliaris and Johansen on many series and tabulates the verdicts
    \item \textbf{Explanation}: a second explanation of the Granger representation theorem, or of a \texttt{VECM} output table
    \item \textbf{Exploration}: candidate pairs on the BVB, or parity conditions for several Central European countries
    \item Example prompt
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \aiprompt{Write Python code that loads monthly US Treasury yields GS1, GS5 and GS10 from FRED, runs the Johansen trace test with a constant and BIC lags, fits a VECM with the chosen rank using statsmodels, and prints beta normalised on the first variables, alpha with t-statistics and the half-lives of the equilibrium errors.}
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Checks you must run}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item The critical values: Engle--Granger (MacKinnon) for residuals, not Dickey--Fuller; Johansen for the right deterministic case
    \item The direction of the null: ``no cointegration'' in Engle--Granger; ``rank $\le r$'' in the trace test
    \item That every series is $I(1)$ before testing, and that a high correlation of levels is not reported as cointegration
    \item The sign of the adjustment coefficients and the half-lives, in the right time unit
    \item Backtests: no look-ahead in pair selection, costs included, the number of pairs tested reported
    \item Every cited reference: it must exist; check the DOI
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Summary}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Key takeaways}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Cointegrated $I(1)$ series share common stochastic trends; a combination $\beta^\top\mathbf y_t$ is stationary
    \item Engle--Granger: OLS in levels, then ADF on the residuals with MacKinnon critical values; check with Phillips--Ouliaris
    \item ECM: changes respond to the lagged equilibrium error; $\gamma$ gives the speed and the half-life
    \item VECM: $\Pi = \alpha\beta^\top$; Granger representation: cointegration $\Leftrightarrow$ error correction; Johansen tests choose $r$
    \item Cointegration helps forecast relations (spreads), not levels; applications must be judged out of sample and after costs
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Key formulas}
\itemsize{\small}
{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.4}\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
\textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{Formula} \\
\midrule
Cointegration & $\mathbf y_t \sim I(1)$, \quad $\beta^\top\mathbf y_t \sim I(0)$ \\
Engle--Granger & $y_t = a + b x_t + u_t$; \quad $\Delta\hat u_t = \gamma\hat u_{t-1} + \sum_j\delta_j\Delta\hat u_{t-j} + e_t$, \quad $H_0$: $\gamma = 0$ \\
ECM & $\Delta y_t = c + \gamma\,\hat u_{t-1} + \delta_0\Delta x_t + \dots + \varepsilon_t$, \quad $h_{1/2} = \ln 0.5/\ln(1 + \gamma)$ \\
VECM & $\Delta\mathbf y_t = \alpha\beta^\top\mathbf y_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\Gamma_i\Delta\mathbf y_{t-i} + \mathbf u_t$, \quad $\Pi = \sum_i A_i - I$, \quad $\Gamma_i = -\sum_{j>i}A_j$ \\
Johansen & $\lambda_{\mathrm{trace}}(r) = -T\sum_{i>r}\ln(1 - \hat\lambda_i)$, \quad $\lambda_{\max}(r) = -T\ln(1 - \hat\lambda_{r+1})$ \\
Equilibrium errors & $\mathbf z_t = \beta^\top\mathbf y_t$: \quad $\mathbf z_t = (I + \beta^\top\alpha)\mathbf z_{t-1} + \dots$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Self-assessment}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: Engle--Granger with two variables gives $\tau = -3.1$ for $T = 300$. Do you reject ``no cointegration'' at 5\%?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: no: $-3.1 > -3.36$; with the Dickey--Fuller value ($-2.87$) you would wrongly reject
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: an ECM gives $\hat\gamma = -0.1$ on monthly data. What is the half-life?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.9 \approx 6.6$ months
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: four $I(1)$ variables have cointegration rank 3. How many common trends drive them?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: $n - r = 1$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Next: \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter8_long_memory_arfima.pdf}{Chapter 8}, long memory: series between $I(0)$ and $I(1)$, fractional differencing and ARFIMA
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
